overview: Gala, also called Gaia, ruled the Massyles of eastern Numidia and was the father of Massinissa. This map record is badly mistimed: its 200 to 100 BCE window begins after Gala’s death, around 206 BCE. The outline lies in northeastern Algeria. The story below distinguishes his third-century kingdom from earlier monuments and the later Numidian life visible in that region.

periods.title: Gala’s last years
periods.summary: Alliance with Carthage countered the growing power of Syphax to the west.

periods.title: A disputed succession
periods.summary: Massinissa recovered his paternal kingdom after rival relatives took power.

periods.title: The imported map’s later century
periods.summary: Massinissa and his successors developed a larger Numidian kingdom. This is later context, not Gala’s reign.

sections.title: A royal family in a wider war

items.text: Livy tells a vivid story about Gala’s grandson Massiva: orphaned, he was brought up by his grandfather, then accompanied his uncle Massinissa to Spain. Captured after joining a battle against orders, he was returned by Scipio. This is a later Roman account of a royal childhood, shaped partly to praise Scipio.

When Gala died, the crown did not pass straight to his son. Livy describes succession through Gala’s brother Oesalces and then Capusa, followed by a violent struggle involving Mezetulus and the young Lacumaces. Massinissa returned from Spain and recovered his father’s realm. Royal family trees could become battlefield maps.

In the following decades, Massinissa’s ambitions reached well beyond his father’s kingdom. He expanded at the expense of both western Numidian rivals and Carthage. Scholars caution that the western conquest sequence is poorly documented; the enormous later kingdom should not be projected backward onto Gala.

An earlier landmark near Batna is the Medracen, a monumental circular tomb with a stepped roof, Doric-style columns and Egyptian-inspired details. Gabriel Camps placed its construction in the later fourth or early third century BCE. It shows the resources and architectural connections of earlier Numidian rulers; the name of its occupant remains uncertain.

Inside the Medracen, an eleven-step stair leads into a long passage. In 1969, Camps examined cedar beams in its roof, including fire-marked timbers; earlier writers had mistaken the construction. Radiocarbon tests on the wood helped investigate the monument’s age. Even a royal tomb depended on skilled carpentry as well as stonework.

Later Numidian Cirta, today Constantine, occupied a rocky plateau protected by the deep Rhummel gorge on two sides and steep ground on another. An approach from the southwest linked it to the Koudiat hill. The landscape helped make the city defensible while shaping how people reached its streets.

A dwelling identified toward Sidi M’cid, beyond Cirta’s main plateau, contained Campanian pottery that dated occupation to at least the first century BCE. A household’s broken dishes can therefore help date a neighborhood. This house belongs after Gala’s lifetime, just after the map’s imported period.

At El Hofra outside Cirta, inscriptions in Punic, Neo-Punic, Greek and Latin preserve traces of a sanctuary and its changing community of worshippers. These finds help recover a city whose ancient remains were heavily damaged by later rebuilding. Different written languages survive where much of the architecture does not.

A small offering stone in the Louvre names Hannibaal, son of Bodmelqart, dedicating a vow to Baal Hammon in thanks for being heard and blessed. The museum dates it between 225 and 50 BCE and tentatively associates it with El Hofra. Here a father’s name helps identify a person otherwise almost lost to history.

The same stone fragment has a carved rudder above a double-moulded panel holding the inscription. Someone planned both the image and the words before cutting the stone. Its careful layout makes a personal act of worship into a surviving example of craft and design.

Under Massinissa in the early second century BCE, Numidian grain surpluses supplied Roman armies overseas. Archaeologists Papi and Martorella calculate more than 2.2 million Roman modii in recorded deliveries during the century’s first thirty years. Behind those royal shipments stood the recurring work of sowing, harvesting, storing and transporting cereal crops.

Written language sample: GYY is the scholarly transliteration of Gala’s name in the Punic text of a bilingual dedication from Dougga, about 138 BCE. It means the personal name Gaia or Gala. This later memorial to his son Massinissa preserves the family relationship; Dougga lies east of this imported outline.

ending.text: Gala’s rule ended with his death around 206 BCE. The ensuing succession struggle eventually brought his son Massinissa back to power; eastern Numidia became part of a larger kingdom. The map’s 100 BCE endpoint marks neither Gala’s death nor the disappearance of Numidian communities.
